Stanford physicists just built an AI memory out of atoms and light.
It's called a Hopfield network: a web of switches that can recall a whole memory from a blurry piece.
Show it a smudged letter, and it settles into the clean one. John Hopfield won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for this idea.
But there's a catch. Store too many memories and the network gets frustrated, and fills up with false ones. Physicists call that a spin glass.
Stanford's Lev lab built that network from cold atoms inside an optical cavity, trading photons back and forth.
In their light-driven version, the false patterns turn into real, reliable memories.
The capacity beat the classic Hopfield limit by up to seven times, in a network of just sixteen spins.
And the atoms physically shift, which mimics how brain synapses briefly rewire while learning. That doubled memory capacity.
It's a tiny prototype, not a product. But it hints at memory machines that run on physics itself.
